planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall with eyes only 1-2 in below the soil surface; established clumps resent disturbance and can remain in place for generations.

directions: This deep crimson, fully double bomb-form heirloom has been documented in European gardens since at least the 1580s and was among the first peonies carried into American colonial and pioneer gardens, earning it the folk name 'Memorial Day peony' for its late-spring bloom timing in many regions. Set divisions shallowly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and avoid crowding by later-emerging perennials, since it breaks dormancy and flowers earlier than most Paeonia lactiflora cultivars. Established clumps need little more than a spring feeding and fall cleanup, and the plant's dense, rounded foliage mound holds ornamental value after bloom. It has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its reliability and longevity in the garden.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit plants

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall with eyes 1-2 in deep; give it room since the single flowers show best when stems are not crowded by neighboring perennials.

directions: Bred by A.P. Saunders from Mons. Jules Elie crossed with the species Paeonia mlokosewitschii, this hybrid was the only successful cross ever produced from that particular pairing and remains prized for its large, cupped, pale creamy-yellow single flowers with prominent orange anthers. It is among the earliest peonies to open each spring, with rounded, crinkled guard petals that hold up well through rain showers. Plant in full sun in deep, fertile soil and resist the urge to divide often, since flowering improves as the clump matures over several seasons. New spring foliage emerges with a distinctive reddish-pink flush before turning green.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall with eyes 1-2 in below the soil surface in a spot with excellent drainage; upright stems rarely need staking.

directions: Introduced by Glasscock and Falk in 1956, this hybrid produces large, upward-facing single blooms of vivid fiery scarlet-red surrounding a dense boss of golden-yellow stamens, aging to a softer pink as flowers mature on the plant. Its sturdy, well-branched stems and light fragrance make it a favorite for cutting, and it received the American Peony Society's Award of Landscape Merit for garden performance. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and avoid deep planting, which delays and reduces flowering. The mid-to-late spring bloom season and vigorous, floriferous habit have kept it in wide commercial production for decades.
sources: American Peony Society Award of Landscape Merit

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall with eyes just below the soil surface; like other Itoh hybrids it forms a shrub-like clump that rarely needs staking or division.

directions: Registered in 1999 by hybridizer Roger Anderson from open-pollinated seed of 'Bartzella', this intersectional (Itoh) hybrid carries semi-double to double blooms that open red and yellow, with outer petals fading toward cream while the inner petals stay red, giving each flower a glowing bicolor effect. The compact, sturdy clump holds its glossy, deeply cut foliage in good form all season after bloom, a hallmark advantage of Itoh types over standard herbaceous peonies. Grow in full sun to light afternoon shade in fertile, well-drained soil; established plants are long-lived and need minimal maintenance beyond a fall cleanup. 'Hillary' received the American Peony Society's 2020 Gold Medal and was named 2021 Peony of the Year.
sources: American Peony Society Gold Medal Award
